title: Starting Strong with the Transformative and Simple Think-Pair-Share Strategy
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart makes the case for Frank Lyman's Think-Pair-Share as the foundational speaking routine of the school year, reporting that it carries roughly eighty percent of the student talk in his classroom. He opens with Harvey Daniels and Nancy Steineke calling it the most instantaneously transformational structure a teacher can add, then explains his own criteria for adopting any strategy: effectiveness and efficiency. Effectiveness means the strategy both teaches content and gives deliberate practice in thinking, reading, writing, speaking and improving; efficiency means it wastes as little of the sixty-minute period as possible, which he frames as a justice issue because a squandered minute a day costs three class periods a year. He then sets out the five-step structure, including an optional feedback and mini-lesson step, warning that skill growth from the routine alone will taper off without instruction and feedback. The rest of the piece lists the opening mini-lessons he teaches alongside it, from the call-to-attention signal to follow-up questions and partner quality. Practical tips follow, including daily seating changes for the first weeks to build the norm that everyone works with everyone. He closes by arguing the conversational skills transfer well beyond school.
points: Stuart's strategy-selection test is explicit and reusable: a routine must teach content and give deliberate skill practice, and it must waste as little instructional time as possible.
He frames wasted minutes as a justice question, calculating that one squandered minute a day equals three lost class periods over a 180-day year for students who can least afford it.
The optional fifth step matters most for growth, since the bare routine raises speaking skill at first and then plateaus without explicit mini-lessons and partner feedback.
He teaches the supporting micro-skills separately across the first weeks, including the call-to-attention signal, follow-up questions and what makes a good partner.
Daily seating chart changes in the opening weeks operationalize the everyone-works-with-everyone norm and let the teacher observe how students mix.
quotes: In order for my students to progress to successful pop-up debates , and to drastically increase the quantity of speaking they'll do during their time in my room, I need to start with the simplest possible training ground for verbal communication: two people having a conversation. Toward that end, the first week of school finds me teaching Frank Lyman's classic Think-Pair-Share routine, and the rest of the weeks of school have me using it for roughly 80 percent of the student speaking that will happen in my room all year.

First, a strategy must effectively do what it is we want it to do. During my school year, I want to provide my kids with two things: first, the opportunity to learn the content set out by my peers and me in our professional learning communities; second, an abundance of opportunities to improve their thinking, reading, writing, speaking, and living abilities (in other words, the five elements of the non-freaked out framework ).

Remember: efficient doesn't mean “rushed”; it means “it gets the job done with as little waste as possible.” And I am a realist when it comes to classroom instructional time: each of the 60 minutes per day that I have with my students is precious; I cannot “let myself off the hook” if I squander a minute of class time per day because, by the end of a 180-day school year, that amounts to 180 minutes or three full class periods .

Before we dive into some specific objectives and tips for teaching Think-Pair-Share at the start of the school year, pause and reflect: are you using strategies that pass both the effectiveness and efficiency tests? What tweaks do you suspect might be possible to increase either or both of those things with strategies you currently use?

While many of these are ideas I've been using for years, I owe a debt of gratitude to Steineke and Daniels for their clarifying, highly practical work in the aforementioned Teaching the Social Skills of Academic Interaction . If you're aiming to build Social-Academic Skills (or the character strengths of social intelligence and interpersonal self-control) this year, Daniels and Steineke's book is immensely practical.

Think-Pair-Share makes us better not just at learning, but important situations like interviewing or dating. These are skills, then, that we all want — and though the work will be hard, it will also be fun as we do it together this year, day in and day out.
